traveler: Fyodor Adrianovich Yevtishchev (Fedor Jeftichew, 'Jo-Jo the Dog-Faced Boy')
title: The Kostroma Forest and the Bowery: a Boy Exhibited, and the Cave That Was Written in New York
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Tenerife, the first recorded hairy family
stops.date_confidence: attested as Gonsalvus's birth year; a precedent stop, not an event in Yevtishchev's life
stops.campa: Petrus Gonsalvus is born on Tenerife with hair over his whole face and is sent as a child to the French court, where he is dressed as a gentleman, taught Latin, and shown. He marries; his children are born hairy too, and the family is passed from court to court as a gift. Three hundred and thirty-one years before Yevtishchev, the sequence is already fixed: the condition, the education, the exhibition, and the hair seen before the man. Reference works on hypertrichosis count about fifty such cases since the Middle Ages.
suggested_refs: Sixteenth-century court portraits of Petrus Gonsalvus and his hairy children, Ambras Castle collection

stops.name: Berezniki near Manturovo, the village birth
stops.date_confidence: contested: Russian Wikipedia gives '1868 or 1870' and this village; English and French Wikipedia give 1868 and Saint Petersburg, 900 km away. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: In the forest country of Kostroma Province, in a village outside Manturovo, a boy is born with fine hair over his face and body. Russian Wikipedia records the village as Berezniki, the year as 1868 or 1870, and the boy's own surname as Petrov. Neither parent is named. No parish register has been found for the birth, in this village or anywhere else, and the whole Russian record of his first years rests on an encyclopedia entry rather than on paper anyone has held. The hair is the one thing about him that no source disputes.
suggested_refs: Parish registers of the Manturovo district, Kostroma Province, 1866-1872, not yet located

stops.name: Saint Petersburg, the other birthplace
stops.date_confidence: attested by English and French Wikipedia; flatly contradicted by Russian Wikipedia, which names Berezniki near Manturovo. Not resolved here.
stops.campa: The account most repeated in English and French puts the birth in the imperial capital instead, in 1868, with no district, street or parish given. Saint Petersburg and the Kostroma villages are nine hundred kilometres apart and the two versions cannot both be true. The atlas prints both pins rather than choose, since choosing would be the first of the many decisions other men made about this life on his behalf. What the versions agree on is the condition: congenital hypertrichosis, present from birth and shared with the man who raises him.
suggested_refs: English and French Wikipedia entries on Jeftichew, which carry the Saint Petersburg birth without a supporting document

stops.name: Korovino near Manturovo, the man who takes him
stops.date_confidence: undated; placed at the earliest plausible point. The adoption is attested by Russian Wikipedia and contradicted by English Wikipedia, which calls Adrian his father outright.
stops.campa: Adrian Yevtishchev, of the neighbouring village of Korovino, is covered in the same fine ash-coloured hair. Russian Wikipedia calls him the boy's adoptive father; English Wikipedia calls him the father, and the two cannot be reconciled. The boy takes his name and loses Petrov, which will surface again a decade later in Europe as what everyone will assume is an invented stage name. Whatever the relation, this is the second hair-covered person in one small district of Kostroma, and that coincidence is the fact the showmen buy.
suggested_refs: Russian Wikipedia's naming of Korovino and Berezniki as the two men's home villages, the only located source for either

stops.name: The Kostroma forest, the hermit story
stops.date_confidence: traditional; undated in the sources, placed before the 1873 European debut
stops.campa: Adrian is said to have fled his village and lived alone in the forest until showmen found him. The story is told by the Human Marvels biography and by Russia Beyond and by nobody holding a document. It is also the seed of everything that follows: the Wild Man of the Kostroma Forest, then the cave, the hunter, the capture, the barking. The billing is written here, in a forest that may never have held him, before either of them has left the empire. What the district actually contained was two hairy men and a livelihood in it.
suggested_refs: The Human Marvels biography of Jeftichew, reachable through its kickassfacts.com reprint and Internet Archive snapshots
sources: Russia Beyond, 'The tragic story of the Russian dog-faced boy'

stops.name: Kostroma, the debut at four or five
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no town is named in any source, and the city of Kostroma stands in for an unrecorded provincial fairground some 230 km from the family's district
stops.campa: On the Russian fair circuit the boy is shown beside Adrian as the son of the Wild Man. He is four, or five; the source gives no town, no fairground, no date beyond the year, and this pin is the nearest identifiable point rather than a place he is known to have stood. He has been on exhibition longer than he has been able to speak in sentences. Whatever the act is paid, someone else is holding it. No account of this earliest touring survives in any language checked for this dossier.
suggested_refs: The Russian provincial fair circuit of the early 1870s, for which no itinerary of the pair has been located

segments.name: The Wild Man of the Kostroma Forest

stops.name: Paris, the Tivoli-Vauxhall
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1870s by French Wikipedia, which names the venue; the month is set to October to match the Figaro notice
stops.campa: On the rue de la Douane, near the Place de la République, the pleasure garden called the Vauxhall de Paris bills the pair as the dog man and his son Fedor. It is not a circus, whatever the English accounts say afterwards; it is an exhibition hall in a garden, and Paris files in to look. Adrian is the act and the boy is the proof that the thing runs in the blood. The billing has already moved them out of Kostroma Province and into a forest of the imagination that no Russian map carries.
stops.quote: L'Homme chien et son fils Fédor
stops.quote_source: Billing at the Vauxhall de Paris, 1870s, recorded in French Wikipedia, 'Fédor Jeftichjew'
suggested_refs: The site of the Tivoli-Vauxhall on the rue de la Douane, now rue Léon-Jouhaux, 10th arrondissement

stops.name: Paris, the correspondent goes backstage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Le Figaro no. 290, 17 October 1873, pp. 3-4
stops.campa: Le Figaro sends the writer who signs himself Un monsieur de l'Orchestre behind the curtain and prints the visit under the title Behind the Scenes with the Dog-Man. It is the earliest document in this life not written to sell tickets, and it is a newspaper feature. Fedor is five years old in it, or seven, depending on which birth year holds. The page images were not opened for this dossier; the article is cited at second hand from two encyclopedias, which agree on the issue number, the date and the title.
stops.quote_source: Un monsieur de l'Orchestre, Le Figaro no. 290, 17 October 1873, pp. 3-4
suggested_refs: Le Figaro no. 290, 17 October 1873, pp. 3-4, in the Gallica digitised run, not consulted directly
sources: Le Figaro no. 290, 17 October 1873, cited in French and English Wikipedia

stops.name: Europe, the decade with no record
stops.date_confidence: no evidence of any kind; the pin is a Berlin placeholder for an interval in which nothing whatever is documented
stops.campa: Between the Figaro notice and his reappearance around 1883 there is nothing. Not a poster, not a playbill, not a passenger list, not a paragraph. Where they went, whether Adrian was alive at the end of it, when the boy began working without him: unknown in every language checked. This pin does not mark a place he was. It marks the width of the hole, dropped on Berlin because Berlin is one of the two cities ever named for the pair, and the atlas would rather draw a gap than smooth it over.
suggested_refs: European exhibition and fairground press, 1874-1882, unsearched for either Yevtishchev in any reachable index
sources: Inference from the absence of citations for this interval in English, French and Russian Wikipedia

stops.name: Berlin, the years as Theodore Petroff
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: English Wikipedia reaches 1883 by adding ten to 1873, which is arithmetic rather than a source. Russia Beyond names Berlin with no date and no venue.
stops.campa: Around 1883 he surfaces performing under the name Theodore Petroff. The name has been read for a century as an invention of the trade. Russian Wikipedia suggests otherwise: Petrov is his own surname, the one he carried before Adrian took him, and if that is right then this is the only stretch of his working life spent under a name that belonged to him. Berlin sees him under it and does not write it down. He is fifteen, and for the first time the act is his rather than his father's.
suggested_refs: Berlin exhibition-hall programmes of the early 1880s, in which the name Theodore Petroff has not been searched for
sources: Russia Beyond, 'The tragic story of the Russian dog-faced boy'

stops.name: Liverpool, the agent from America
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the Human Marvels biography; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01, and no hall in Liverpool is named
stops.campa: A talent agent working for P. T. Barnum sees Theodore Petroff perform in Liverpool and recruits him for America. The pin sits at the docks, the era's chief embarkation point for the Atlantic, which is a plausible landmark and not a place any source puts him. He is fifteen, or sixteen, depending on which birth year is right. No hall in the city is named, and the recruitment survives in a single popular biography rather than in a contract or a press notice.
suggested_refs: Liverpool music-hall and exhibition bills of 1883-1884, unsearched for the name Theodore Petroff

stops.name: Castle Garden, the landing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no document names his point of entry. Castle Garden was New York's immigrant depot until 1890, which makes it near-certain. The month is arbitrary.
stops.campa: The immigrant depot at the tip of Manhattan takes in nearly every European act bound for Barnum's show in these years, Ellis Island being six years from existing. No manifest naming him has been found, so this stop is inference from practice rather than from paper. He arrives able to speak Russian, German and English. He will spend the next twenty years being advertised as a creature that cannot speak at all, and the two facts sit in the same encyclopedia paragraph without touching.
suggested_refs: Castle Garden arrival records for 1884, not searched for any of his six recorded names
sources: Reconstruction from 1884 transatlantic arrival practice; no source names his point of entry

stops.name: New York, the name Barnum gives him
stops.date_confidence: year attested by English Wikipedia; month unrecorded and set for sequence
stops.campa: Barnum renames him Jo-Jo the Dog-Faced Boy, and that name outlives every other one, including the two that may have been his. The atlas has been carrying the dog-headed men a long time before he arrives: Saint Christopher, the baptized cynocephalus of the Passion of Marmarica, over whom Ratramnus of Corbie wrote asking whether the dog-headed peoples of the north could take the sacraments; and the Barahnakar, the dog-faced people Ibn Battuta reported in the eastern ocean. Jo-Jo is that same figure, ticketed.
suggested_refs: Barnum lithograph posters for Jo-Jo the Dog-Faced Boy, 1884 onward

stops.name: The Kostroma forest, the cave that never was
stops.date_confidence: the fabrication is attested as fabrication by English Wikipedia, which flags the Barnum material as invented; the date is the publicity season, not an event
stops.campa: Barnum's copy sends a hunter into the forest near Kostroma to track two savages to a cave and take them alive. Adrian is printed as uncivilizable. The boy is coached to bark and growl on cue, and does. This pin marks a place where nothing happened, because the story told about it moved more tickets than the truth and is still the version most people meet first. The forest is real and the district is real. The cave was written in an office in New York.
stops.quote: Wild Man from the Kostroma Forest
stops.quote_source: Adrian Jeftichew's billing from 1873, recorded in English Wikipedia, 'Fedor Jeftichew'
suggested_refs: Barnum promotional material on the cave capture, flagged as fabrication in the encyclopedia record itself
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Fedor Jeftichew' (Barnum promotional material, flagged there as fabrication)

stops.name: New York, three languages and a bark
stops.date_confidence: undated skill, placed at the point the record first mentions it
stops.campa: He speaks Russian, German and English. The record notes it without comment, in the same breath as the growling. Nothing in any source says what he thought of the arrangement, whether he negotiated it, what share of the gate he saw, or whose idea the barking was. He leaves no letters, no interview, no memoir, no signature. Everything anyone knows about his voice is that it worked in three languages and that people paid to hear it do something else instead.
suggested_refs: No first-person document by Yevtishchev has been located in any language; this is the file's central absence

stops.name: Madison Square Garden, the spring season
stops.date_confidence: the Garden residency is attested for the show and never for him by name. The first building stood 1879-1890, so this stop cannot run past 1889/90; an earlier pass on this file gave 1884-1891, which is impossible.
stops.campa: Barnum's Grand Traveling Museum, Menagerie, Caravan and Circus opens its New York season each spring at the Garden raised on the site of Barnum's own old Hippodrome, at the north-east corner of Madison Avenue and 26th Street. Jo-Jo takes his place among the acts. The residency is documented for the show and not once for him personally in a named year, which is how nearly the whole American decade reads. The building comes down in 1890 and a second Garden opens on the site that June.
suggested_refs: The first Madison Square Garden, Madison Avenue and East 26th Street, demolished 1890

stops.name: 229 Bowery, Eisenmann's studio
stops.date_confidence: the studio operated at this address into the late 1880s and closed in 1898; the sitting itself is undated
stops.campa: Charles Eisenmann photographs nearly every sideshow performer of the age at his Bowery studio, and Jo-Jo sits for him. The cabinet card that results is the image most people have seen: a boy in a braided tunic, hands at his sides, looking straight into the lens. Sixteen photographs of him survive in the public archives, by Eisenmann, by Fred Park Swasey, and by the Lumière studio around 1875 with Adrian beside him. They are the closest thing to a document he left, and he did not write them.
suggested_refs: The sixteen surviving photographs in the Wikimedia Commons category 'Fedor Jeftichew'

stops.name: The Globe Museum, twenty-three shows in a day
stops.date_confidence: attested by Garland Thomson without a year; placed mid-decade. The museum's exact address is not established in the source, and the Bowery dime-museum pin stands in.
stops.campa: At the Globe Museum in New York his manager works him twenty-three shows in a twelve-to-fourteen-hour day. The figure comes from an academic collection on the exhibition of the extraordinary body, and it is the hardest single fact in the American years, harder than any tour date. Everything else in this decade is billing, reconstruction or a photograph. This is a number, and it describes roughly thirty-five minutes between performances from opening to close, for whatever the manager chose to hand over.
suggested_refs: Rosemarie Garland Thomson, ed., Freakery: Cultural Spectacles of the Extraordinary Body (NYU Press, 1996), p. 317
sources: Rosemarie Garland Thomson, ed., Freakery (New York University Press, 1996), p. 317

stops.name: Bridgeport, the winter quarters
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Barnum's Bridgeport winter-quartering is well documented for the show, and no source places Yevtishchev there
stops.campa: Between seasons the show goes home to Barnum's own city, where the menagerie, the wagons and the people wait out the cold until the route opens again. Whether Jo-Jo wintered there or in a New York boarding house is recorded nowhere. The reconstruction is offered as reconstruction. Where he slept for four months of every year is a small thing to have to guess at, and no source names the house, the street or the company he kept in any winter of the American years.
suggested_refs: The Barnum & Bailey winter quarters at Bridgeport, Connecticut
sources: General Barnum & Bailey operating history; no source names Yevtishchev at Bridgeport

stops.name: Louisville, one of the most interesting freaks alive
stops.date_confidence: the 1886 notice is reported by Russia Beyond without naming the paper, town or date; Louisville is a placeholder for the state, and wire syndication means the item need not reflect an appearance in Kentucky at all
stops.campa: A Kentucky newspaper calls him one of the most interesting freaks alive. The outlet reporting this names neither the paper nor the town, and syndication in the 1880s carried such notices into places the show never entered. The phrase is kept anyway, because it is the only line of American press about him quoted in any reachable source, and because of what it takes for granted about the category it files him under. Newspapers.com, which would settle it, is behind a paywall this pass could not cross.
stops.quote: one of the most interesting freaks alive
stops.quote_source: Unnamed Kentucky newspaper, 1886, quoted in Russia Beyond, 'The tragic story of the Russian dog-faced boy'
suggested_refs: Kentucky newspapers of 1886, unidentified and unsearched; the notice survives only as a quotation
sources: Russia Beyond, 'The tragic story of the Russian dog-faced boy'

stops.name: Philadelphia, the eastern swing
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the documented Barnum & Bailey route; no source names a Philadelphia engagement for him
stops.campa: The show moves by rail on a route settled months in advance, a city a day down the eastern seaboard, canvas up at dawn and down by midnight. Philadelphia is a fixture of it. No source puts Jo-Jo in Philadelphia by name; no source puts him anywhere by name in these years except a Bowery museum and a photographer's studio. The route is drawn because a map showing only the places a newspaper happened to mention would be a falser picture of a touring life than one that admits the circuit.
suggested_refs: Barnum & Bailey route books for the 1880s, which list towns and dates but not sideshow personnel
sources: General Barnum & Bailey touring-circuit history; no source names him at Philadelphia

stops.name: New York, the Greatest Show on Earth
stops.date_confidence: attested: Barnum and Bailey combined their shows on 28 March 1881, and the joint name dates from 1888, when the partners rejoined after a split. An earlier pass on this file dated the merger 1887, which corresponds to neither event.
stops.campa: Barnum and Bailey, who first combined in 1881 and then split, come back together and put the name on everything: Barnum & Bailey Greatest Show on Earth. It is the banner Jo-Jo performs under for the rest of his American career and the one that carries him back across the Atlantic at the end of the century. The corporate fact is documented to the year. His place inside it is documented not at all, which is the standing condition of this whole section of the map.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'P. T. Barnum', for the 1881 combination and the 1888 renaming after the partners' split

stops.name: Chicago, the western turn
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the documented route; no source names a Chicago engagement for him
stops.campa: Chicago anchors the route west and the show plays it every year it goes that way. He is billed by now as Jo-Jo the Dog-Faced Man, the boy having become inaccurate; no source gives a year for the change, and both versions run in the posters for a while. He has been on exhibition since before he could read, in two empires and a republic, and there is no record of his ever having done anything else for money. This stop is the circuit rather than a documented engagement.
suggested_refs: Barnum & Bailey posters billing Jo-Jo as Dog-Faced Boy and Dog-Faced Man, undated in the transition

stops.name: Boston, the standard stop
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the documented route; no source places him at Boston
stops.campa: Boston takes its turn on the eastern circuit. The show arrives in the small hours, unloads at the rail yard, parades to the lot and opens at two. The sideshow annex runs continuously alongside the big top, and that is where he works. The ring belongs to other men; his room is the tent the crowd files through in a line, looking. No document from Boston names him. What the reconstructed stops preserve is the shape of the work rather than its dates.
suggested_refs: The sideshow annex arrangement of the Barnum & Bailey tented show, in which Jo-Jo worked rather than in the ring
sources: General Barnum & Bailey touring-circuit history; no source names him at Boston

stops.name: Brooklyn, the near rounds
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the documented route; no source names him at Brooklyn
stops.campa: Brooklyn's showgrounds take their turn on the New York rounds, close enough to the Garden that the same crowd can come twice. Nothing in the record places him here in particular, as nothing places him anywhere at all in these years. The route stops describe the arithmetic of the work: a few minutes of being looked at, repeated through a city a day across a continent for twenty years, in front of people who paid once and remembered it for the rest of their lives.
suggested_refs: Brooklyn showgrounds used by the Barnum & Bailey circus on its New York-area rounds
sources: General Barnum & Bailey touring-circuit history; no source names him at Brooklyn

stops.name: Washington, the capital
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from the documented route; no source names a Washington engagement for him
stops.campa: The Greatest Show on Earth plays the national capital as a matter of course. He is somewhere in the annex, in a tunic with braid on it, between whatever acts the manager set on either side of him. No document from Washington names him. By now his face has been reproduced in a popular science magazine, in a dermatological treatise and on cabinet cards sold by the thousand, and the same photograph serves the medical literature and the ticket booth with no alteration at all.
suggested_refs: The identical use of Eisenmann-era photographs in medical plates and in circus publicity

stops.name: Midway Plaisance, the Columbian Exposition
stops.date_confidence: attested for Muybridge's hall and for the Midway's exhibits; no source places Yevtishchev on the Midway, and shared ground is not a meeting
stops.campa: Along the mile of the Midway Plaisance the World's Columbian Exposition sets its human-curiosity and ethnological exhibits in a row, and Eadweard Muybridge opens the Zoopraxographical Hall among them to sell moving pictures of a horse. Two trades stand side by side that summer: the machine that proves what the eye cannot catch, and the tent that charges to look at a man. No source puts Jo-Jo on the Midway. The atlas records the ground they share and does not invent the meeting.
suggested_refs: The Midway Plaisance concessions of 1893, whose human-curiosity exhibits shared the strip with Muybridge's hall
sources: General history of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition Midway

segments.name: The Greatest Show Goes to Europe

stops.name: London, the tour opens
stops.date_confidence: the tour's December 1897 start is attested by Wikipedia; London's inclusion and his presence on the tour are both reconstructed
stops.campa: Bailey takes the whole apparatus across the Atlantic in December 1897 for five years, and London is among the capitals it plays. Yevtishchev's presence on the tour is reconstruction: the dates are attested, his name on them is not. He is about thirty, and returning to the English circuit that sold him thirteen years earlier. Joseph Pilates comes into this same music-hall and travelling-circus economy fifteen years later, in London and on the Blackpool piers, and works it until a war closes it.
suggested_refs: Barnum & Bailey's 1897-1902 European tour, whose dates are documented and whose personnel lists are not

stops.name: Berlin, the great circus building
stops.date_confidence: the Steiner lecture is attested to this day; the Barnum & Bailey Berlin season and Yevtishchev's presence on it are reconstructed
stops.campa: Berlin keeps large fixed circus buildings, Busch and Renz, the kind of hall a touring American show fills for a season. In one of them, on the twenty-fourth of June 1900, Rudolf Steiner stands in front of seven thousand printers and speaks to them about the working life. The building is a circus for the rest of the year. The atlas has no document putting Yevtishchev in Berlin on this tour and claims none; what it has is a city where the same rooms held the lecture and the menagerie inside a single season.
suggested_refs: Circus Busch and Circus Renz, the Berlin circus buildings that hosted both touring shows and mass meetings

stops.name: Paris, twenty-eight years later
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed stop on the attested 1897-1902 tour; no source confirms a Paris engagement for him on this leg
stops.campa: The tour brings him back to the city that first wrote him up as the dog-man, when he was five and the act belonged to Adrian. Almost nobody in the Vauxhall crowd of 1873 will be in these seats. He is the property of an American corporation now instead of a Russian showman, billed in English, and the thing being sold has not changed in twenty-eight years. No source confirms he played Paris on this leg; the reconstruction rests on the tour's dates and on Paris being unavoidable.
suggested_refs: Paris seasons of the Barnum & Bailey European tour, undocumented for individual sideshow performers

stops.name: Vienna, the least supported stop on this map
stops.date_confidence: speculative: no source names Vienna for this tour or for him. This is the weakest point in the file and is flagged rather than quietly dropped.
stops.campa: Vienna is a customary capital for touring American circuses of the period, and that sentence is the entire evidence for this stop. No document names the city on the 1897 to 1902 itinerary, and none names him anywhere on the continent in these years. It is included, and labelled, because the alternative is a five-year European tour drawn as three cities. A reader should treat this pin as a guess with a tag on it, and weigh it against the four stops in this segment that at least rest on a tour with dates attached.
suggested_refs: Vienna circus and variety press, 1897-1902, unsearched; the stop rests on no source at all
sources: Reconstructed itinerary for the Barnum & Bailey European tour; no source names Vienna

stops.name: New York, the brief return
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: only the tour's 1902 end date is attested. The return itself rests on one popular biography's phrase and names no venue, date or ship. An earlier pass tagged this attested; it is not.
stops.campa: The five-year tour ends and the show comes home. A popular biography says he briefly returned to the United States to rejoin the circus before going abroad again, and that sentence is the whole of the evidence: no venue, no date, no ship, no season. The atlas prints it as reconstruction. What is certain is only that he is somewhere in Europe again within two years, working, and that he does not cross the Atlantic a third time. Two years later he is dead in an Ottoman port.
stops.quote: briefly returned to the United States to join up with the Barnum and Bailey's Circus
stops.quote_source: thehumanmarvels.com biography, via the kickassfacts.com reprint
suggested_refs: Barnum & Bailey's 1902 return to the United States, documented for the show and not for him

stops.name: Salonica, the illness
stops.date_confidence: the illness is attested; no date is given for its onset, and January is taken from the death
stops.campa: He is in Ottoman Salonica, apparently still touring, and he takes pneumonia. No source names the circus he is with, the hall he is playing, the house he is lodged in, or a single person who is with him. He is about thirty-five and has been on exhibition for roughly thirty-one of those years: in the Russian empire, in a Paris pleasure garden, in German halls, in American annexes, and now in a port at the far edge of the Balkans where nobody has written down why he is there.
suggested_refs: Ottoman Salonica's variety and circus venues of 1903-1904, unidentified for this engagement

stops.name: Salonica, the death
stops.date_confidence: contested by one day: English Wikipedia gives 31 January 1904, French and Russian Wikipedia both give 1 February 1904. Two against one, unresolved. Place, cause and age agree across all three.
stops.campa: He dies of pneumonia. Three encyclopedias give the place, the cause and the age identically and split on the day, two of them putting it twenty-four hours later than the English record that everyone cites. The atlas prints the English date and carries the objection in the hedge, because a life this thoroughly narrated by other people should not have its last fact quietly settled by whichever version happens to be written in the most-read language.
suggested_refs: Ottoman civil or consular death records for Salonica, January-February 1904, unsearched

stops.name: Salonica, the grave that is not recorded
stops.date_confidence: no evidence: no burial record has been found in any source consulted, and the date is nominal
stops.campa: No cemetery. No plot. No marker. No burial register, genealogy index or grave database consulted for this dossier returns anything for him at Thessaloniki, and no source says who claimed the body or whether anyone did. Whether a marked grave ever existed is unknown. The record of a man photographed sixteen times, printed in a science magazine and a medical treatise, and looked at by hundreds of thousands of paying strangers stops at the pneumonia and does not resume.
suggested_refs: Thessaloniki burial registers of 1904, in which no search has returned him
sources: Absence across Find A Grave-type indexes and genealogy search results consulted in 2026

stops.name: New York, the medical plates
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Popular Science Monthly plate is of 1874 and the dermatological treatise illustration of 1888. Placed in this segment though the first predates most of his career.
stops.campa: Popular Science Monthly reproduces him in 1874 as a specimen, and a dermatological treatise does it again in 1888. The caption in the medical literature and the word on the sideshow banner are the same word. Reference works on hypertrichosis still list him among the small set of historically documented cases, dates given as 1868 to 1904, alongside Petrus Gonsalvus three centuries before him. Science and the annex tent used the same photograph, and neither of them asked him anything.
suggested_refs: Popular Science Monthly vol. 4 (1874), plate 'PSM V04 D465 Fedor Jeftichjew'

stops.name: Hollywood, the recurring face
stops.date_confidence: attested films of 1940, 1995 and 2017; the pin stands for the studio industry rather than a located event, and the date is the first of the three
stops.campa: Strike Up the Band names him in 1940. The X-Files rebuilds him from an edited photograph in the 1995 episode Humbug. The Greatest Showman puts him back on a Barnum stage in 2017, in a film about the man who bought him. Each version stands further from any document than the one before it, and each is seen by more people than ever paid at the annex. The barking, coached into a teenager who spoke three languages, has become a costume note. He is played, each of those times, by an actor who takes the hair off afterwards.
suggested_refs: The X-Files, 'Humbug' (1995), whose Jeftichew image is a doctored period photograph

stops.name: Hollywood, the Chewbacca tradition
stops.date_confidence: unverified tradition: no primary Lucasfilm design source attests it. The 1977 date belongs to the film, not to the claim, which is recent.
stops.campa: A modern popular-history claim, repeated by outlets that do not source it, holds that his face shaped the design of Chewbacca. No Lucasfilm design document has ever been produced for it, and the atlas records the claim as tradition rather than fact. It is kept for what it shows about the shape of his afterlife: the last thing he is still supplying, more than a century after the pneumonia, is a face for something that is not a person. Nobody repeating the claim names the villages, the birth year, or the twenty-three shows.
suggested_refs: Lucasfilm design records for Chewbacca, in which no Jeftichew reference has been produced
sources: All That's Interesting, article on Fedor Jeftichew (accessed via web search, 2026); tagged as unverified tradition

stops.name: Washington Square, the academy arrives
stops.date_confidence: attested: Garland Thomson, Freakery, New York University Press, 1996, p. 317
stops.campa: Ninety-two years after the pneumonia, a university press publishes a collection on the cultural exhibition of the extraordinary body, and page 317 records the twenty-three shows a day at the Globe Museum. It is the only academic treatment of him anyone has located, and it gives him a page. There is no critical edition and no monograph in English or Spanish. There are no collected letters either, because there are none to collect. The hardest number in his working life reaches the scholarship as one line inside somebody else's argument.
suggested_refs: Rosemarie Garland Thomson, ed., Freakery (NYU Press, 1996), the sole academic treatment located
sources: Rosemarie Garland Thomson, ed., Freakery (New York University Press, 1996), p. 317

stops.name: Moscow, the country that forgot him
stops.date_confidence: undated: the Russia Beyond piece carries no date in the reachable version, and 2020 is nominal for the twenty-first-century rediscovery
stops.campa: Russian-language outlets run rediscovery pieces on him in this century, introducing a Kostroma-born performer to readers who have never heard of him and whose fame was entirely American. The framing is the nineteenth-century circus freak with a rare disease. The Russian record is also the only one that gives him a village, an adoption and a surname of his own, which is more than the language he was famous in has managed in a hundred and twenty years.
suggested_refs: Russia Beyond, 'The tragic story of the Russian dog-faced boy', undated in the reachable version
sources: Russia Beyond, 'The tragic story of the Russian dog-faced boy'

stops.name: Berezniki near Manturovo, the register nobody has opened
stops.date_confidence: no date: this stop marks a present-day absence, and the year is nominal
stops.campa: The parish registers of the Manturovo district for the late 1860s have not been searched, or have been searched and not reported. Until one of them yields a name, the birth stands at 1868 or 1870, in this village or in Saint Petersburg, to parents nobody has named, of a boy whose own surname may have been Petrov. Every other fact in his life was written down by someone selling tickets. The one document that would have been written by someone with no interest in him at all has not been found.
suggested_refs: State Archive of Kostroma Oblast, parish registers of the Manturovo district, 1866-1872
sources: Stated gap: no primary Russian record located in any language
